newsitem.title: USA: NAPM sees moderate manufacturing growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: NAPM sees moderate manufacturing growth in 1997.

text.p: Economic growth should accelerate next year, the nation's purchasing managers said Tuesday, noting they expected a drop in raw material costs early in the year but a small rise in labour costs for all of 1997.

The National Association of Purchasing Management, in its semiannual forecast, said manufacturers expected revenues to rise 5.4 percent in 1997, compared to a 4.9 percent rise expected for this year and a 7.4 percent increase for 1995.

The Tempe, Ariz.-based group of executives who buy everything from acid to zinc for about 300 major corporations, also predicted that prices paid for materials would fall 0.5 percent in the first four months of 1997 but be unchanged for all of the year.

Meanwhile, labour and benefit costs were expected to grow 2.8 percent, the group said. Its surveys are closely watched as gauges of manufacturing and the economy. Manufacturing accounts for about a quarter of the domestic economy.
"There's still a growth trend in manufacturing activity, but it's beginning to bubble down," Ralph Kauffman, chairman of the group's Business Survey Committee, said in an interview.

The best scenario for manufacturers would be continued slow growth with no rise in interest rates next year, he said. "A continuation of the present scenario would be about the best they could expect right now."
He said the group's members were more optimistic now than a year ago, "with 80 percent of them expecting business in the first half of 1997 to be better than or the same as the second half of 1996."

The group forecast that imports and exports would grow next year, with exports growing at a faster clip. A drop in exports contributed to a record trade deficit of $48 billion in the third quarter, the Commerce Department said in a separate report.
Purchasing executives predicted capital spending will fall 1.6 percent in 1997 while production capacity will increase 5.8 percent.

They said they expected stronger holiday retail sales in 1996 compared with 1995, but not as strong as in 1994. Of the respondents, 55 percent saw average holiday sales, while 44 percent forecast "good holiday sales."
The group's members also said the dollar would rise against the German mark and Japanese yen in 1997, which could tend to dampen export growth.

Half said the dollar will rise against the yen and 45 percent said it will strengthen vs. the mark. Only 27 percent saw the dollar weakening against the yen while 22 percent saw it falling against the mark.
Separately, Kauffman said he will leave his post on Jan. 2, 1997. He will be succeeded by Norbert Ore, currently a purchasing director for Sonoco Products Co.
